paragraphs.text: This cake carries the [7572](7572:definition) mark. It is the ripe recipe Menghai Tea Factory first made in the mid 1970s, and other ripe cakes are often described by how they compare with it. The [four digits are a code](7572:reading-the-number): 75 for 1975, the year the recipe began, 7 for the leaf grade that makes up most of the blend, and 2 for Menghai. The number names a whole blend, [not a rank of quality](7572:recipe-not-quality), and the 75 dates the recipe, not the cake. This one was pressed in 1999, from leaf grown in Menghai County.

That year falls in the third decade of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition), twenty-six years after Yunnan’s state factories brought [wet piling](shou:wet-piling) into production in 1973. At twenty-seven years the cake is well past the ten that the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, so storage has shaped it as much as the years have.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
